question: Which L2 regularization strength produces the best cross-validated logistic regression model?
rationale: L2 regularization is a standard technique for improving model generalization. We test a range of values spanning orders of magnitude to find the optimal tradeoff. Cross-validation with 5 contiguous folds (no shuffle) provides an unbiased estimate of generalization performance. Brier score is appropriate for probabilistic classification evaluation.
decision: Select lambda with the lowest 5-fold cross-validated Brier score across [0.0, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0]
expected_effect: We expect to identify a lambda value that improves upon the baseline (lambda=0). The improvement magnitude will indicate whether regularization is beneficial. If no improvement, lambda=0 is selected and improvement_over_baseline=0.
falsifier: If all tested lambda values produce identical or meaningless Brier scores (e.g., all NaN), the implementation is faulty.

question: Do product interaction features improve logistic regression performance?
alternatives: Include raw features plus products (x0*x1, x1*x2, x2*x3, x0*x3)
rationale: Interaction features can capture non-linear relationships. We compare models using paired t-test across folds to determine statistical significance. A threshold of t > 2.0 provides a reasonable cutoff for practical significance given 5 folds (df=4).
decision: Fit both representations with lambda=0.1, compute per-fold Brier differences (raw - interaction), perform paired t-test. Set interaction_helps=true only if t > 2.0.
expected_effect: If interactions are meaningful, the raw model's Brier will be consistently higher (worse) than the interaction model, producing a positive t-statistic. If not, t may be small or negative. The boolean result will reflect whether this signal is strong enough to recommend inclusion.
falsifier: If paired t-test fails (e.g., degenerate variance), the implementation needs adjustment. If Brier scores are not numeric across all folds, the models are invalid.

question: Which sparsity-quantization configuration best preserves dense model performance?
rationale: Model compression is evaluated by retention = dense_brier / compressed_brier. Higher retention indicates better preservation of performance. Sparsity removes smallest-magnitude weights; quantization discretizes remaining weights. We fit the dense model once on all data with lambda=0.1, then apply compression to the same weights.
decision: Fit dense model with lambda=0.1 on full dataset. Apply each (sparsity, bits) pair to the trained weights. Compute in-sample Brier for each compressed model. Select the configuration with highest retention.
expected_effect: Less aggressive compression (lower sparsity, higher bits) should retain more performance. We expect a tradeoff where very aggressive compression (60% sparsity, 4 bits) degrades performance more than modest compression. The best config will achieve high retention.
falsifier: If all compressed models perform worse than dense (retention < 1.0 is normal), but if some have invalid Brier scores or if retention differs by more than 100x between configs, the compression logic is suspect.
